title: Amy Poehler and Michael Schur's 'Dig' Is No 'Parks and Rec'—But It's Still a Fun Trip
author: Judy Berman
body:
Dig is sure to catch the eye of anyone scanning for signs of a post-midterms vibe shift. (Never mind that it was announced last spring, just a few months into a second Trump term some interpreted as a long-term rightward swerve.) The Peacock comedy, whose 10-episode first season arrives on Nov. 23, reunites Amy Poehler and Michael Schur, the duo behind the ultimate Obama-era sitcom: Parks and Recreation. But instead of embracing any zeitgeist, it seems to be in flight from the burden of relevance.

Escapism is baked into its premise like designs on ancient pottery shards. Created by Poehler and Schur, who adapted it from a 2023 novel by Kate Myers, Dig follows a team of excavators at an archaeological site in Greece, where they spend summers unearthing artifacts in sweltering heat. While the dominant genre is workplace comedy, a comfortable format for Schur (Brooklyn Nine-Nine, The Office), the show is also a sun-soaked romance and a madcap mystery. The uneven execution of these elements, as well as some mild miscasting and uncertain stakes, keep it from achieving the flow state of peak Parks and Rec. Let go of inflated expectations, however, and its pleasant characters and novel setting yield a satisfying trip.

One thing the show has going for it is the kind of multigenerational cast we rarely see in TV’s workplaces. Leading the dig is the plummy-voiced, blue-blooded, elder-statesman archaeologist Neville Wycombe, played to perfection by Hugh Laurie. As he approaches his 70s, Neville keeps promising to retire and promote his hypercompetent deputy, Elise (Poehler). “If I have one concern, it’s about your demeanor,” he tells her. The head of an operation that relies on dozens of fickle undergrads for its manual labor needs to know how to make that labor enjoyable and inspiring. This (in addition to fundraising, naturally) has always been Neville’s specialty. Elise, though? “You know my motto,” she reminds the town’s hunky mayor, Stavros (Kayvan Novak, best known as Nandor from What We Do in the Shadows), with whom she has a history of hooking up: “Work hard and never have fun.”

Neville may be a charismatic presence, but Dig’s warm heart beats for its women. Just as she did alongside Daniel Radcliffe and Steve Buscemi in Miracle Workers and as a libidinous teen in Blockers, Geraldine Viswanathan gives a scene-stealing performance as Dylan, a wild child returning to the dig years after an abrupt departure that hurt Elise, her mentor, as well as her then boyfriend Gary (Jon Pointing). Almost 30 and aware that her impetuousness now looks less like mystique and more like mess, she’s hoping to repair both relationships. But she didn’t anticipate Gary would be engaged to Clare (Antonia Thomas), whose commitment to her work and upper-crust restraint make her everything Dylan could never be. Into this social morass stumbles Patty (Fina Strazza), Neville’s dizzy hayseed of a teenage assistant. What Kenneth the Page was to 30 Rock, Patty is to Dig.

After Elise flubs a big speech, scolding the kids she was supposed to be welcoming, Neville steps in, to the cheers of his young admirers, and agrees to return for one more year. So when she and Dylan accidentally make a major discovery, she’s primed to go along with her old friend’s risky proposition that they keep the find quiet until their excavation is complete so that Neville can’t claim all the credit. Clare and Patty are soon in on the conspiracy too. Of course, in a place where everyone is gossiping about, if not sleeping with, everyone else, secrets of this magnitude don’t stay secret for long.

Although they share a work ethic befitting ambitious women in realms ruled by complacent men (shout out Ron Swanson), Elise is not meant to be Poehler's cheerful Parks and Rec powerhouse Leslie Knope in a sweat-soaked bandanna. Characters talk about her as though she radiates badass allure, an edge honed by being chronically underestimated. Kathryn Hahn or Lizzy Caplan would be natural fits for the role; Poehler is a smidge too sunny, even when you can tell she's trying not to be.

It doesn’t help that scripts packed with smart jokes and deft twists default to cuteness just when the romance plots should be heating up. Elise and Stavros are funny in a lost-in-translation way (it takes her a beat to realize that when he refers to her “behind that continues to be employed,” he means her “butt that just won’t quit”), but his Greece’s Greekest Greek character is thin. The Dylan-Gary-Clare triangle would've benefitted from evidence that the Boy Scout type at its center has chemistry with either woman. Schur’s most beloved couples (Leslie and Ben, The Good Place’s Eleanor and Chidi) tend to be sweet more than sexy. In this steamy setting, though, lust should come with the territory.

Dig suffers from the sense that it isn’t exactly about anything in the way Parks and Rec was about the noble, thankless work of civil servants or The Good Place grasped for moral guidance in a world gone mad. I got the sense, as the season progressed, that the creators had more to say in defense of a resource-starved field that connects us to our human past, instead of propelling us into our copiously funded, high-tech future. It would’ve been exciting to see more of the passion for archaeology that drives people like Elise make it onto the screen.

Hopefully, Poehler and Schur will get more time to do that. His best shows have had bumpy starts, made crucial changes early, and flourished soon after, deepening characters and relationships until fictional people felt like real friends. This one has the same potential. It’s already a breezy watch, with a fresh premise and ample charm. The core of intergenerational friendships between women is solid, too; if the romance doesn’t work, it needn’t play such a big role in subsequent seasons. Like the ancient humans its characters study, Dig has the tools it needs to thrive. Now it has to learn to use them.
